title: Dismaying climate news doesn’t mean the climate fight is over
summary: In this issue of our environmental newsletter, we look at what the recent bad news about climate change means for future warming; see the structure of a unique type of lake that is gone for good in…

image.caption: Individuals have the power to advance climate action, scientists say, such as how they vote or even through protest. (Sean Kilpatrick/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Welcome to our weekly newsletter where we highlight environmental trends and solutions that are moving us to a more sustainable world.

Hi, it’s Nicole. I often joke that I write a lot about doom-and-gloom climate change, things such as the warmest years, rising ocean temperatures, etc. But even I had to take a pause when a couple of dire reports were released at the beginning of September. It made me think that perhaps people felt that they are powerless and that the end is nigh. So I wanted to remind people that all is not lost.
This week:

blocks.text: Dismaying news doesn’t mean the climate fight is over
There were a few climate stories that came out recently that were, well, not great news.

First there was the United Nations Environment Programme’s (UNEP) report on Sept. 2 that found we will overshoot the 1.5 C threshold set out by the Paris Agreement within the next few years. That threshold aims to limit the dangerous impacts of a warming world.

Then, on Sept. 4, the federal government released its second edition of Canada’s Changing Climate Report, which found that the country could face an average 5 C of warming by 2081 to 2100 relative to 1850 to 1900.
These stories sound dire, and, to be fair, they are. They are an indication that, as we continue to pump fossil fuels into the atmosphere, we will continue to warm.
But that doesn’t have to be the end of the story.
Just because we will surpass 1.5 C doesn’t mean it has to stay that way. And just because Canada could face 5 C of warming by the end of the century doesn’t mean it has to.

Bill Hare, CEO of Climate Analytics, a global climate science and policy institute, welcomed the UNEP report, but, in a news release, said he was concerned that it didn’t do a good enough job of explaining that there is a way out, and that the report risks turning "into a call to apathy rather than a call to arms."
I was intrigued with that statement and decided to reach out to him.

"I think that's the main message that … if we just treat this fatalistically, that, oh well, we busted through one-and-a-half, we're going to have to learn how to cope with three degrees — I don't think that's going to work. I think that that's a recipe for apathy. It's very fatalistic," he told me.
"The message needs to be that we can still rescue this 1.5 limit. We can still get back below it. But it's going to take urgent action and in particular on fossil fuels."

Government regulations on greenhouse gas emissions or creating green projects are big ways that change can happen. But what happens when people elect someone who they believe will make those changes but doesn't?
"I think people need to think about what they do next time when they vote," he said.

If you don’t follow climate scientist Katharine Hayhoe — who is the chief scientist for the Nature Conservancy and a professor at Texas Tech University — you should. She is a big advocate of climate action, not climate doom.
She says most people don’t realize that we’ve already made a difference.

"When the Paris Agreement was signed, we were heading for four- to five-degree Celsius of warming by the end of the century. Now we're heading to a 2.7-degree warming by the end of the century, globally, if we just continue on our current pathway," she told me.

Following its report, UNEP director Inger Andersen told journalists that even if we’re currently on track to pass 1.5 C of warming, that it "is still the goal," as reported by Euractiv, a European media network.
"But now, we need to approach it differently, from above," she said, saying there would need to be "rapid and deep cuts" to fossil fuel emissions.
After that, she said, we can aim for "net negative emissions," meaning we remove more greenhouse gases than we emit.
So we don’t have to remain at 1.5 C. We can move the dial backward. And if more urgent action is taken — climate scientists and UNEP say — there is hope.
"For me, the definition of hope is, if we do something, will it make a difference?” Hayhoe said. “And the science says, yes, if you do something, it will make a difference."
— Nicole Mortillaro

The Big Picture: RIP to Canada's last lake of its kind
Scientists have confirmed in a new study that Canada's last epishelf lake is gone.

Jérémie Bonneau, the lead author and an assistant professor at Laval University in Quebec City, said its loss is sad, as the Milne Fiord epishelf lake on Ellesmere Island in Nunavut was "the last thing like that in Canada."
"Suddenly, it's … drained away and then everything that was living in there is gone."
The diagram below shows how the lake, made up of freshwater floating on saltwater, formed.
You can read more here about the lake and what its demise says about the irreversible changes transforming the Arctic in a warming climate.
— Emily Chung

The Toronto International Film Festival is underway, and the Climate Film Festival is underway in New York. The festival's founder recommends seven climate-related films to stream online on services like Netflix, YouTube and Apple TV, from documentaries to biopics to animated kids movies.

One YouTuber’s stubborn quest to bring a wrecked $6 million Bugatti hypercar back from the dead has turned into a very public fight over planned obsolescence and how manufacturers restrict ownership at a massive environmental cost.
Check out this cookie made from plastic bottles that have been transformed by yeasts into edible proteins and flavouring molecules. People gave it high marks for aroma.

As you stock up on Halloween chocolate, you’re probably feeling it costs way more than it used to. A new study says blame it on the rain, and expect it to have more of an impact as we warm the planet more.

blocks.text: Flood protection installed under Saskatoon park
After three summers of construction to help address flooding, Hugh Fraser embraced the reopened Brevoort Park as he stood Tuesday on new grass near newly planted trees.
Fraser gave credit to himself and his neighbours for pressuring the city to open the park a month early so people could enjoy the restored space before the snow falls.

The retired Saskatoon resident joined a group of about 20 people, most of whom were city officials, to mark the reopened park, which now lies atop a concrete basin large enough to accommodate enough water to fill two Olympic-sized swimming pools.

The restored south part of the park, which is located in the Brevoort Park neighbourhood, becomes the fourth completed project as part of a $54-million multi-year city hall plan to prevent flooding in certain neighbourhoods.
"The residents of Brevoort Park are very happy that the park is finally open," Fraser said in an interview. "It took a long time, but it turned out perfect."
Fraser said he was surprised more of his neighbours failed to turn out for the event, given the length of time the park was closed for the project.

However, the flood basin is already proving its worth, according to a city news release, which says the storage system under the park captured an Olympic-size pool of water during a rainstorm on Labour Day.
The storage tanks can hold 8.6 million litres and fill up during rainstorms so that the storm sewer system does not become overwhelmed and water doesn't pool on the streets and wind up in basements.
Russ Munro, director of Saskatoon Water, says 41 homes will be protected from flooding by the Brevoort Park project.
Mayor Cynthia Block recalled her early days as a city councillor when "devastated" residents came to city hall after a flood event.
"The loss was incredible — the amount of damage that was done to their homes," Block told those gathered. "And it was going to be repeated and repeated and repeated and repeated."
Block said she felt "defeated" trying to deal with flooding.

However, she learned about a federal program to address flooding while attending a conference and brought it to the attention of city administration. The federal government is providing $21.6 million toward the city's program.
The system under Brevoort Park represents the first project of its kind in which the infrastructure is hidden underneath a park.

The three other completed projects are known as dry ponds, in which the surface of the park is sunken and usable most of the time, but fills up during flooding and then drains to take the strain off the storm sewer system.

Those dry ponds are located in W. W. Ashley District Park, Churchill Park and Weaver Park. A fourth dry pond is mostly complete in Cumberland Park. There are four other flood strategy projects underway and on track to be completed by next year.
— Phil Tank
